context: pavement-led · airfield ground lighting (AGL) & navaids under live-airport possession windows

brief.intro: New to this project type? Airside works build the pavement aircraft actually move on — runway, taxiway and apron — plus a small, specialised electrical scope: airfield ground lighting (AGL), the power supplies that feed it, and navigation aids. Most of the schedule is earthworks and pavement, not building MEP. What makes it different from a road is that almost every activity near a live or partially-live airfield only happens inside a granted possession — a fixed block of hours or a night when air traffic control lets you onto that surface. Pavement strength and curing time are physical constraints you cannot compress; possession availability is the operational constraint you plan around.

scope.name: Enabling & site works
scope.desc: Clearance, setting out, and coordination with airport operations before any physical work starts.

scope.name: Earthworks & subgrade
scope.desc: Cut/fill to formation level and subgrade compaction/proof-rolling under the pavement.

scope.name: Airfield drainage
scope.desc: French drains, interceptors and attenuation carrying surface water off the paved area.

scope.name: Pavement
scope.desc: Base and sub-base courses, then the PQC (rigid concrete) or asphalt surface courses for runway, taxiway and apron.

scope.name: Airfield Ground Lighting (AGL)
scope.desc: In-pavement and elevated edge/centreline fixtures wired in specialist series circuits.

scope.name: Primary electrical power
scope.desc: Constant-current regulators (CCR), duct banks and substations feeding the AGL circuits.

scope.name: Navaids & met systems
scope.desc: Civil and cable interfaces for navigation aids (ILS/PAPI) and meteorological sensors.

scope.name: Fuel hydrant system
scope.desc: Underground hydrant pit network for aircraft refuelling, where the scope includes it.

scope.name: Markings & signage
scope.desc: Pavement markings and taxiway/runway guidance signage.

scope.name: Testing & commissioning
scope.desc: AGL photometric checks, CCR energisation, and the calibration flight check that proves the system to a live aircraft.

glossary.plain: airfield ground lighting — the runway/taxiway edge and centreline lights that guide pilots.
constant-current regulator — a specialist power supply feeding AGL lights in a series circuit, not a normal LV panel.
pavement quality concrete — the rigid concrete pavement used on runways and aprons.
the finished subgrade level the pavement structure is built on.

must_get_right: It is a possession-led programme — the real driver is how many hours or nights of live-surface access you are granted, not labour or plant availability.
Pavement strength and curing time are fixed by the concrete or asphalt mix design — do not compress them; they gate every trade that follows on that panel or section.
AGL and CCR power are a specialist series-circuit system, not conventional LV wiring — book the specialist subcontractor and the calibration flight check early.
Coordinate every trench, duct and pit with airport operations — nothing crosses an active surface without an approved possession.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Activities are tied to pavement panel or section numbers so progress can be tracked by area; the network is calculated (F9) with total float kept ≥ 0 in the baseline.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Earthworks and pavement construction run extended daytime shifts on unrestricted areas. Duct-bank, AGL and any tie-in work on or near a live surface runs only within approved night possession windows governed by NOTAM — a separate possession calendar drives those activities, not a standard working week.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: The driving path runs subgrade → pavement base/sub-base → PQC or asphalt surface course (curing time fixed by mix design) → duct banks & AGL fixture install → CCR terminate & energise → photometric survey → flight check → handover. Possession-window availability for airside tie-ins is usually the real constraint on progress, not resourcing.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: Phasing is agreed with airport operations in advance; a single mobilisation; no live-traffic diversions beyond the agreed plan; and the pavement mix design is frozen before production paving starts.

sections.heading: Key quantities & possession windows
sections.body: The programme is sized by pavement area and possession windows rather than by long-lead equipment; AGL fixtures and CCR units are the only meaningfully long-lead procurement and are noted here alongside the possession-critical quantities.

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Airside access requires escort and security clearance and is coordinated with live air traffic control; specialist paving and AGL subcontractors are scarce and often shared across phases; plant movements are restricted to designated haul roads and crossing points.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Principal risks: possession windows lost to weather or airport operations, pavement not reaching load-bearing strength in time for the next lift, and calibration-flight aircraft availability. Schedule contingency is held immediately before the flight check and before final handover.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3 by pavement section; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for night possessions — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
